assessment_summary: A proof attempt would fail because the statement is fundamentally false. While greedy coloring is bounded by $\Delta(G)+1$, the number of colors used can be arbitrarily large even for bipartite graphs where $\chi(G)=2$. Thus it is not bounded by $\chi(G)+1$. A standard counterexample is the crown graph $H_{n,n}$ (a complete bipartite graph $K_{n,n}$ minus a perfect matching, with parts $U=\{u_1..u_n\}, V=\{v_1..v_n\}$). Its chromatic number is 2. If we process the vertices in the order $u_1, v_1, u_2, v_2, \dots, u_n, v_n$, the greedy algorithm assigns color $i$ to both $u_i$ and $v_i$. This uses $n$ colors. For $n \ge 4$, the number of colors used is $n > 3 = \chi(G)+1$. Therefore, the claim is invalid.
counterexample: Crown graph $H_{n,n}$ (bipartite, $\chi(G)=2$) ordered $u_1, v_1, \dots, u_n, v_n$. It uses $n$ colors, which is greater than $\chi(G)+1=3$ for $n \ge 4$.
